title: De Oratione Et De Octo Partibus Orationis [Attributum]
author: Cassiodorus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1188.tmp1188.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: quam elocutionem docuimus necessario ex nomine verboque constare. Deinde quod ex caeteris partibus orationis nequaquam plena est elocutio, ut si dicamus ante templum, et non jungamus ambulo, pendet oratio. Nam cum dicimus, Cicero scripsit, orator docuit, quod certe ex nomine et verbo per se plenum est
passages.english: we have shown that an utterance necessarily consists of a noun and a verb. Next, an utterance is by no means complete from the other parts of speech: if we say "before the temple" and do not add "I walk", the sentence hangs [unfinished]. For when we say "Cicero wrote", "the orator taught", this is certainly complete in itself from a noun and a verb.

passages.original: Nomen, quod ex familia venit, ut Anicius. Cognomen, quod proprie nostrum est, ut Sylla, Catilina. Agnomen, quo aut er virtute, aut ex vitio aliquo utimur : ex virtute, ut Africanus, qui vicit Africam; ex vitio, ut Naso, quod grandem nasum habuit; unde dicitur Ovidius Naso; Sura, quod a sura grandi dicitur, ut Publius Lentulus Sura. Me- minerimus autem non necesse esse ista quatuor pro- priorum generum nomina simul inveniri.
passages.english: The *nomen* [family name] is what comes from the family, such as Anicius. The *cognomen* is what is properly our own, such as Sulla, Catiline. The *agnomen* is one we use on account of some virtue or some fault: from virtue, as Africanus, who conquered Africa; from a fault, as Naso, because he had a large nose, whence Ovid is called Naso; Sura, which is said from a large calf [of the leg], as Publius Lentulus Sura. But let us remember that it is not necessary for these four kinds of proper names to be found together.
passages.notes: "er virtute" read as "ex virtute". Calling Catiline's name a cognomen and the illustrations generally follow the text as given.

passages.original: Feminina quoque tres formas habent; exeunt enim aut per eis, aut per ias, aut per ne, ut Atreis, Atrias, Atrine, ut apud Virgilium, Nerine Galatea. Sane considerandum est quia patronymica Graeca cujus- cunque generis Graeca melius regula proferuntur.
passages.english: Feminines also have three forms; for they end either in -eis, or in -ias, or in -ne, as Atreis, Atrias, Atrine, as in Virgil, "Nerine Galatea". Indeed it should be noted that Greek patronymics of whatever gender are better produced by the Greek rule.

passages.original: at quae in sor exeunt feminina in trix non mittunt : quae vero in tor, necesse est ut feminina in trix minant, ut pro- curator, procuratrix. Hoc si a verbo venerit in tor scilicet terminatum, necesse habuit femininum in trix mittere, et facere auctrix; sed quia non dicatur auctrix, Virgilius testatur dicens : Auctor ego sum videndi.
passages.english: but those that end in -sor do not form feminines in -trix, whereas for those in -tor it is necessary that they form feminines in -trix, as procurator, procuratrix. If this [word] came from a verb, ending namely in -tor, it would have had to form a feminine in -trix and make auctrix; but that auctrix is not said, Virgil bears witness, saying: "I am the author (auctor) of seeing."
passages.notes: "minant" read as "mittant". The argument is elliptical: the Virgil quotation apparently shows auctor used of a female speaker. The quotation as given does not match any known Virgil line exactly; text may be corrupt.

passages.original: Quaeritur enim utrum acris dicatur, an acer; con- stat autem hodie utrumque dici, de viro, ut in Vir- gilio : Humero Pelops insignis eburno acer. Acris vero de femina dicitur, ut apud Horatium : Solvitur acris hiems.
passages.english: For it is asked whether acris or acer should be said; it is agreed today that both are said: [acer] of a man, as in Virgil: "Pelops, distinguished by his ivory shoulder, keen (acer)". Acris, however, is said of a female, as in Horace: "Keen (acris) winter is loosening."

passages.original: quia de qualitate sumus in- terrogati, unum aliquid ex illis trinus dicimus, aut doctus, aut pulcher est, aut mendicus; non dices a qualitate longus est, aut brevis. Quando enim inter- rogamur, quantus est? non possumus respondere nisi a mensura, aut longus, aut latus, ant brevis est. Nec nos terreat quod Virgilius dixit quantitatis nomen ad animam applicans : Magnanime AEnea; sed hic Grae- cum voluit imitari; non quia quantitas ab animo ve- nerit, sed qualitatem animi per quantitatem laudare voluerit.
passages.english: because we were asked about quality, we say some one thing from among those three, either he is learned, or handsome, or a beggar; you will not say, from quality, he is tall or short. For when we are asked, how big is he? we can only answer from measure: he is tall, or broad, or short. Nor should it alarm us that Virgil said, applying a noun of quantity to the soul, "great-souled Aeneas"; but here he wanted to imitate the Greek, not because quantity comes from the mind, but because he wanted to praise the quality of the mind through quantity.
passages.notes: "ex illis trinus" taken as "ex illis tribus"; "ant" as "aut".

passages.original: ut si vel mus dicere, Dulcius est mare Ponticum quam caetera; nullum enim mare non modo dulcius est, sed ne dulce quidem. Inveni- tur saepe ita comparativus, ut vim positivi suscipiat, ut apud Virgilium : Senior Charon, sed cruda Deo viridisque senectus fuit; sed senior pro eo quod est senex ponitur; non enim alter fuerat Charon, cujus comparatione hic senior vocetur.
passages.english: as if we were to say, "The Pontic Sea is sweeter than the others"; for no sea is not only sweeter, but not even sweet. The comparative is often found so as to take on the force of the positive, as in Virgil: "the elder Charon, but the god had a fresh and green old age"; but "elder" is put for "old"; for there had not been another Charon, in comparison with whom this one could be called elder.

passages.original: Cum vero per superlativum praeferre voluerimus, qui certe servit genitivo tantum plurali, praeponere cum suo tantum generi debemus, et dice- re : doctissimus orator oratorum, doctissimus gram- maticus grammaticorum. Verum illud non nos turbet, quia legimus superlativum servire genitivo singulari, ut apud Virgilium, ditissimus agri, fortissimus gen- tis; sed haec 596 quamvis sono singularia sint, ta- men intellectu pluralia sunt. Nam cum dicimus di- tissimus agri, fortissimus gentis, intelligendum est quia res ista ex pluribus constet.
passages.english: But when we want to prefer [someone] by means of the superlative, which certainly governs only the genitive plural, we must set him before his own kind only, and say: "the most learned orator of orators", "the most learned grammarian of grammarians". But let this not disturb us, that we read the superlative governing the genitive singular, as in Virgil, "richest of the land", "bravest of the race"; for these, though singular in sound, are yet plural in sense. For when we say "richest of the land", "bravest of the race", it is to be understood that this thing consists of many.
passages.notes: "596" is a page number from the edition, omitted.

passages.original: Genera nominum sunt sex : masculinum, ut hic Cato; femininum, ut haec musa; neutrum, ut hoc monile; commune duorum generum, ut hic et haec sacerdos : trium generum, ut hic, et haec, et hoc felix; epicoenon, quod Latine promiscuum dicitur, ut passer, aquila.
passages.english: The genders of nouns are six: masculine, as hic Cato; feminine, as haec musa; neuter, as hoc monile [necklace]; common of two genders, as hic and haec sacerdos [priest/priestess]; of three genders, as hic, haec and hoc felix [happy]; epicene, which in Latin is called promiscuum, as passer [sparrow], aquila [eagle].

passages.original: aut feminina, ut musca; aut neutra ut to- reuma, quod Graecum est. Nullum enim Latinum no- men neutrum in a terminatur in nominativo singulari, excepto uno Thoria, quod nomen est fluminis, quod- que apud Sallustium lectum est; aut communia, ut rana, advena.
passages.english: or feminine, as musca [fly]; or neuter, as toreuma [embossed work], which is Greek. For no Latin neuter noun ends in -a in the nominative singular, except one, Thoria, which is the name of a river and which is read in Sallust; or common, as rana [frog], advena [newcomer].
passages.notes: "Thoria" as a river name in Sallust is unidentified; the reading may be corrupt.

passages.original: Nomina in o vocalem exeuntia in nominativo, aut masculina sunt, ut Cicero; aut feminina, ut imago·
passages.english: Nouns ending in the vowel o in the nominative are either masculine, as Cicero, or feminine, as imago.

passages.original: Sunt eliam nomina quae nominativum singularem et pluralem similes habent, ut nubes, dies, quae propter hoc dicta sunt numero communia. Sunt etiam nomina non habentia numerum pluralem, ma- sculina, ut pulvis; non enim dicuntur pulveres, quamvis apud Horatium legimus : Novennales dis- sipare pulveres. Sunt item generis masculini tantum pluralia, ut Quirites.; quamvis legerimus, hunc Qui- ritem, ut. quis te redonavit Quiritem? Sunt item ge- neris feminini tantum singularia, ut pax, lux, quam- vis legerimus has paces, has luces.
passages.english: There are also nouns which have the nominative singular and plural alike, as nubes, dies, which for this reason are called common in number. There are also masculine nouns that have no plural number, as pulvis; for one does not say pulveres, although we read in Horace: "to scatter the nine-year dust (pulveres)." There are likewise nouns of masculine gender only plural, as Quirites, although we have read hunc Quiritem, as in: "who has restored you as a Quiris?" There are likewise nouns of feminine gender only singular, as pax, lux, although we have read has paces, has luces.

passages.original: si vero fuerit hoc nomen, ut, quasi diem festum signi- ficet, tantum numeri pluralis erit. Sane sciamus quod his nominibus qu e non admittunt numerum Singularem, apponimus masculinis uni, femininis unae, neutris una; dicimus enim uni cancelli, unae nuptiae, una moenia, ut apud Terentium, ex unis nuptiis geminas mihi facias; et apud Sallustium : hi postquam in una moenia convenere. Sciamus vero quod superflue loquimur, quando dicimus : homo unus advenit; siquidem jam praedictus homo unum significat.
passages.english: But if this noun is such that it signifies as it were a feast day, it will be of plural number only. Let us certainly know that to those nouns which do not admit the singular number we add uni for masculines, unae for feminines, una for neuters; for we say uni cancelli, unae nuptiae, una moenia, as in Terence, "out of one wedding (unis nuptiis) you would make me two," and in Sallust: "these, after they had come together within one set of walls (una moenia)." But let us know that we speak redundantly when we say homo unus advenit ("one man arrived"), since the aforesaid homo already signifies one.
passages.notes: 'qu e' read as 'quae'. The opening clause continues the preceding discussion of Saturnalia; 'ut' seems superfluous.

passages.original: in plurali vero numero, cum tamen scriptum sit per unum l, sic declinatur. Sunt nomina quibus dum in elocutione utimur, alia genitivum casum ducunt, ut ignarus belli, sive bellorum; alia dativum tantum, ut amicus bono, quanquam Terentius in nominativo casu jun- xerit dicens : Amicus meos summus popularis Getha. Alia accusativum, sed per figuram, ut praescius fu- tura, recte enim dicitur, ut praescius futurorum; alia ablativum, ut dignus munere, mactus virtute; alia septimum casum, ut secundus a primo, nam non possumus dicere secundus primo, aut secundus primi, vel secundus primorum, aut tale aliquid.
passages.english: but in the plural number, although it is written with a single l, it is declined thus. There are nouns which, when we use them in speech, some take the genitive case, as ignarus belli or bellorum ("ignorant of war/wars"); others the dative only, as amicus bono ("friend to the good"), although Terence joined [it] with the nominative case, saying: "my greatest friend, [my] fellow countryman Geta." Others the accusative, but by a figure, as praescius futura ("foreknowing the future things"), for it is correctly said praescius futurorum; others the ablative, as dignus munere ("worthy of a gift"), mactus virtute ("honoured for virtue"); others the seventh case, as secundus a primo ("second from the first"), for we cannot say secundus primo, or secundus primi, or secundus primorum, or anything of the sort.
passages.notes: The opening clause, cut off from its context, presumably refers to mille/milia; its sense is uncertain. 'meos' and 'Getha' are the edition's spellings of meus and Geta.

passages.original: Secunda declinatio est quae genitivum singularem per i profert; et est generis masculini et feminini, et neutri, ut Virgilius Virgilii, fraxinus fraxini, prandium prandii. Sciendum plane est quod in hac declinatione omnia nomina genitivum singularem per unum i proferunt, exceptis his quae in ius fuerint terminata, facit enim Mercurius Mercurii;
passages.english: The second declension is that which produces the genitive singular in i; and it is of masculine, feminine and neuter gender, as Virgilius Virgilii, fraxinus fraxini, prandium prandii. It must clearly be known that in this declension all nouns produce the genitive singular with a single i, except those which end in ius, for Mercurius makes Mercurii;

passages.original: Tertia declinatio est quae genitivum singularem per is syllabam profert, est enim generis mascu- lini, feminini, neutri, ut Cicero Ciceronis, Juno Ju- nonis, marmor marmoris; est etiam communis, ut sacerdos sacerdotis, est etiam trium generum, ut demens hujus dementis. Ista haec tertia declinatio nominativum singularem terminat modis quadraginta uno : in a, in e, in o, in c, in t, in al, in el corre- ptum, in il correptum, il ol productum, in ul corre- ptum, in an, in en correptum, in en productum, in on productum, in ar utrumque, in er correptum, in er productum, in or et in ur utrumque, in as et in es productum, in es correptum, in is utrumque, in os correptum, in os productum, in us productum, in us correptum, in ax et in ex correptum, in ex produ- ctum, in ix et in ox correptum, in ox productum, in ux correptum, in ux productum, in ans et in ens pro- ductum tantum, in ons correptum, et in ons produ- ctum, in uns productum.
passages.english: The third declension is that which produces the genitive singular in the syllable is; it is of masculine, feminine and neuter gender, as Cicero Ciceronis, Juno Junonis, marmor marmoris; it is also common, as sacerdos sacerdotis; it is also of three genders, as demens, genitive dementis. This third declension ends the nominative singular in forty-one ways: in a, in e, in o, in c, in t, in al, in short el, in short il, in long ol, in short ul, in an, in short en, in long en, in long on, in ar of both [quantities], in short er, in long er, in or and in ur of both [quantities], in as and in long es, in short es, in is of both [quantities], in short os, in long os, in long us, in short us, in ax and in short ex, in long ex, in ix and in short ox, in long ox, in short ux, in long ux, in ans and in ens long only, in short ons, and in long ons, in long uns.
passages.notes: 'il ol productum' read as 'in ol productum'. The list as printed does not obviously total forty-one.

passages.original: nam venit ab ablativo singulari in i terminato, qui ipse per i toties exit, cum nominativus singularis per is fuerit terminatus, genitivus singularis parem numerum syllabarum per is miserit, ut hic ignis, hujus ignis, ab hoc igni; quamvis Lucanus dixerit igne viam scandens : exceptis tribus nominibus, ut hic mensis, juvenis, canis. Aut cum nominativus singularis, in is terminatus,600 fuerit generis com- munis, ut hic et haec agilis; aut cum nominativus singularis in e correpta fuerit terminatus in genere neutro, et ablativum per i mittat;
passages.english: for it comes from the ablative singular ending in i, which itself ends in i whenever the nominative singular ends in is [and] the genitive singular puts out an equal number of syllables in is, as hic ignis, huius ignis, ab hoc igni—although Lucan said igne, "climbing the way by fire"—except three nouns, namely hic mensis, juvenis, canis. Or when the nominative singular ending in is is of common gender, as hic et haec agilis; or when the nominative singular ends in short e in the neuter gender and puts out the ablative in i;
passages.notes: The syntax of the first sentence is loose; 'toties ... cum' understood as 'whenever'. The numeral '600' is a page number, omitted.

passages.original: Sed hoc sciendum est, quod cum talia occurrunt nomina, ad alia nos his similia conferre debemus, quorum declinatione docti sumus, etiam ista simili ratione declinemus : ut puta, si nesciamus utrum horum Vulcanaliorum an Vulcanalium faciat, ponamus econ- trario sedile nomen, quod habet in ablativo casu singulari sedili, et ad hanc collationem incipiamus declinare, ut haec sedilia, horum sedilium, haec Vul- canalia, horum Vulcanalium; quamvis contra hanc artem possit dici Vulcanaliorum, quomodo anciliorum, dicente Horatio : Anciliorum nominis et togae obli- tus est.
passages.english: But this must be known: that when such nouns occur, we ought to compare them with other nouns similar to them, whose declension we have learned, so that we may decline these too on a similar principle. For example, if we do not know whether it makes horum Vulcanaliorum or Vulcanalium, let us set against it the noun sedile, which has sedili in the ablative singular, and on the basis of this comparison let us begin to decline: haec sedilia, horum sedilium, haec Vulcanalia, horum Vulcanalium; although against this rule one could say Vulcanaliorum, like anciliorum, as Horace says: "he has forgotten the shields (anciliorum), the name and the toga."

passages.original: Nominativus in Latinis aut in a terminatur, ut musa; aut in e, ut sedile; aut in i, ut frugi; aut in o, ut Cicero; aut in u, ut cornu; aut in l, ut mel; aut in um, ut scamnum; aut in en, ut carmen; aut in r, ut puer; aut in s, ut doctus; aut in x, ut pix; aut in t, ut caput; aut in c, ut halec : cujus declinatio in dubitationem cecidit;
passages.english: The nominative in Latin words ends either in a, as musa; or in e, as sedile; or in i, as frugi; or in o, as Cicero; or in u, as cornu; or in l, as mel; or in um, as scamnum; or in en, as carmen; or in r, as puer; or in s, as doctus; or in x, as pix; or in t, as caput; or in c, as halec, whose declension has fallen into doubt;

passages.original: huic siqui- dem in nominativo nominis litteram non invenimus t, fact autem dici non potest, quia nullum nomen re- periri potuit duabus mutis terminatum, undo posset facere lactis apposita t littera in nominativo singulari; lacte solum remansit, quod quasi ex arte diceretur, quod terminetur quasi nomina neutri generis, ut monile, sedile et extera hujusmodi nomina; et au- ctoritate Plauti, qui dixit : sicut lacte lactis simile est : sed quamvis non arte, sed ex auctoritate firme- tur, tamen sciendum est quod hodie usu ita loqui de- beamus, quomodo locutus est Virgilius :
passages.english: since indeed we do not find the letter t in the nominative of this noun; and fact cannot be said, because no noun could be found ending in two mutes, from which it could make lactis by adding the letter t in the nominative singular. Only lacte remained, which would be said as if by rule, because it ends like nouns of neuter gender, as monile, sedile and other nouns of this kind; and [it is supported] by the authority of Plautus, who said: "as milk (lacte) is like milk (lactis)." But although it is confirmed not by rule but by authority, it must nevertheless be known that today in usage we ought to speak as Virgil spoke:
passages.notes: 'undo' read as 'unde', 'extera' as 'cetera'. The Plautus quotation as given is garbled; sense approximate. The Virgil quotation is cut off.

passages.original: Sed constat quia nomen majorem sibi significationis vindicet par- tem. Vim enim suam tunc pronomen obtinet, quando praecesserit nomen; ut si dicamus, Cicero defendit Roscium; ipse eliam Syllam, ilic enim, ipse, sic est positum, tanquam si de novo repetissemus Cicero : sed pro illo nomine propter fastidium iterationis no- minis pronomen videtur inventum.
passages.english: But it is agreed that the noun claims for itself the greater part of the meaning. For the pronoun obtains its force when a noun has preceded, as if we say, "Cicero defends Roscius; he also [defends] Sulla"; for there "he" is placed just as if we had repeated "Cicero" anew. But the pronoun seems to have been invented in place of that noun because of the tedium of repeating the noun.

passages.original: et ex illi causa ista pars sibi hoc nomen spe- cialiter sumpsit, quod hac frequenter utimur in ora- tione. Nam frequenter in sermone composito duo verba invenimus, unum nomen, vel unum partici- pium; ut puta, Virgilius habet recitare; ecce, habet et recitare duo verba sunt : illae sunt singulares partes.
passages.english: and for that reason this part took this name specially for itself, because we use it frequently in speech. For in composed speech we frequently find two verbs, one noun, or one participle; for example, "Virgil has to recite": see, "has" and "recite" are two verbs; they are single parts.
passages.notes: "ex illi causa" read as "ex illa causa". The passage begins mid-sentence; the sense of "one noun, or one participle" in relation to the example is unclear.

passages.original: Regula adverbiorum talis est, ut nomen quod in dativo casu singulari in o fuerit terminatum, in e mittat, ut huic docto, docte; si in i, in ter mittit ad- verbium, ut huic sapienti, sapienter. Sed hanc infir- mavit regulam auctoritas; nam dixit Virgilius, san- guinei lugubre rubent, pro lugubriter; et Terentius, parce ac duriter urgebat, pro dure. In dativo manent, ut falso, vel sedulo : sed faciunt adverbia false, se- dule. Quaedam contra faciunt, ut a duro, duriter;
passages.english: The rule of adverbs is this: a noun which ends in o in the dative singular makes [its adverb] in e, as huic docto, docte; if in i, it makes the adverb in ter, as huic sapienti, sapienter. But authority has weakened this rule; for Virgil said sanguinei lugubre rubent ("blood-red, they glow mournfully"), for lugubriter; and Terence, parce ac duriter urgebat ("he pressed sparingly and harshly"), for dure. Some remain in the dative, like falso or sedulo; but they [also] make the adverbs false, sedule. Some do the opposite, as from durus, duriter;

passages.original: Sed hanc regulam tenere debemus, ut, quoties nominativus in us syllaba fuerit terminatus, tunc secundum genitivum melius dicamus, ut puta Adrumetus, Adrumeti sum; quoties aliter, secundum dativum dicimus, ut Carthago, Car- thagini sum. Sed etiam hoc confundit auctoritas; Sallustius, Narbone consilia Gallorum, pro Narboni; et Virgilius : Tyria Carthagine, quae nunc exspectat, pro Carthagini. De propositio adverbiis non applica- tur. Caeterum soloecismus est, si dicamus de mane; mane adverbium est, de autem praepositio. Nec nobis praejudicant illa adverbia dehinc, desubito, si uno pro- feruntur accentu.
passages.english: But we ought to hold this rule: whenever the nominative ends in the syllable us, then we better speak according to the genitive, for example Adrumetus, "I am at Adrumetum (Adrumeti)"; whenever otherwise, we speak according to the dative, as Carthago, "I am at Carthage (Carthagini)". But authority confounds this too: Sallust [wrote] Narbone consilia Gallorum ("the plans of the Gauls at Narbo"), for Narboni; and Virgil: Tyria Carthagine, quae nunc exspectat ("at Tyrian Carthage, which now awaits"), for Carthagini. A preposition is not applied to adverbs. Otherwise it is a solecism if we say de mane ("from early"); for mane is an adverb, but de is a preposition. Nor do those adverbs dehinc, desubito count against us, if they are pronounced with a single accent.
passages.notes: "De propositio" read as "Praepositio". The Virgil quotation is of uncertain wording as given.

passages.original: itaque veneno illum occidi, non ferro, ne agnosci possit, ratio est : causalis, si illum occi- dero, habebo tunicam; rationalis, itaque veneno illum occidi, ne agnosci possit. Sed hanc rationem mutat auctoritas; nam et Virgilius conjunctionem pro alia posuit dicens : subjectisque urere flammis, pro ve.
passages.english: "therefore I killed him with poison, not with the sword, so that he could not be recognized" is the reason. Causal: "if I kill him, I shall have the tunic"; rational: "therefore I killed him with poison, so that he could not be recognized." But authority changes this principle; for Virgil too put one conjunction for another, saying: subjectisque urere flammis ("and to burn with flames placed beneath"), for -ve.
passages.notes: Virgil's -que is said to stand for -ve ("or").
